passage:
Rain hammered the bus-stop roof, and the school bus was already twenty minutes late. Tanvir kicked a puddle.
"At my old school the bus was never late," Tanvir told Damini, the girl from the new class who shared the shelter. "And everybody was friends. Nobody ever fought."
Damini shrugged. "Nobody?"
"Nobody. It was the best class in the world."
While digging for a dry handkerchief, Tanvir pulled out an old rough notebook. On the back page, in big angry letters: NEVER SHARING MY TIFFIN WITH THAT BENCH AGAIN!! Below it was a drawing of a cross face.
Tanvir stared at it, then quickly shut the notebook. "That was just one day," Tanvir mumbled, as the bus splashed round the corner.

qa.q: What was written on the back page of Tanvir's old notebook?
qa.a: NEVER SHARING MY TIFFIN WITH THAT BENCH AGAIN!!, with a drawing of a cross face below it.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir insist the old class never fought?
qa.a: Tanvir misses the old school and feels unsettled in the new one, so from far away the old class feels perfect and the quarrels have faded.

qa.q: How could a parent help Tanvir without arguing?
qa.a: They could say it's fine to miss old friends, then ask about an ordinary day there, good and grumpy bits, and about one nice thing in the new class. 🙂

qa.q: How might Damini feel hearing that the old class was the best in the world?
qa.a: Damini might feel the new class is being compared unfairly, or that Tanvir isn't ready to give it a chance yet.

grounding: A child who changed schools calls the old class perfect until an angry note in an old notebook shows the forgotten quarrels.

passage:
Vinita pressed her forehead against the balcony grille of their new flat in Bengaluru, watching the colony kids play cricket below.
"In Kolkata, my class was like a family," she said. "We did everything together. Sports day, tiffin, everything."
Her little brother Tejas looked up from his jigsaw. "You cried about Mouli every week. She said your drawing was ugly."
"That never happened."
"And the time the whole class blamed you for the broken window."
Vinita opened her mouth, then closed it. She did remember the window, a little: standing alone by the staff room, cheeks hot.
"It was still nice," she said, quieter.
"Some of it," Tejas agreed, and fitted in a piece.
Downstairs, a girl waved up at the balcony. Vinita hesitated, then waved back.

qa.q: Which city did Vinita's family move from?
qa.a: Kolkata; they now live in a new flat in Bengaluru.

qa.q: What does Vinita's quieter 'It was still nice' suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: Vinita feels wistful and homesick for her old class, but she is starting to recall the hard moments too and admit it wasn't perfect.

qa.q: What could help Vinita settle into the colony?
qa.a: Saying yes to small chances like the girl's wave, and letting herself miss Kolkata while giving new friends a fair try.

qa.q: How does Tejas see his sister's story about Kolkata?
qa.a: Tejas remembers the weekly tears and the window blame, so to him 'like a family' leaves a lot out.

grounding: A girl who moved cities remembers her old class as a family, and her brother reminds her of quarrels she has smoothed away.

passage:
"Uma Didi, my old school had the best teacher in the world."
"Better than Mrs Rao here?"
"Way better. Miss never shouted."
"Pankaj, you told me on the phone last year she made you stand outside for talking."
"That was only once. Maybe twice."
"And the football team? You said they never passed to you."
"They passed sometimes." Pankaj pulled at a thread on the sofa cushion. "It just feels like everything was nicer there."
"It feels like that because you miss it. Missing something is allowed."
"Then why do I only remember good stuff?"
"Because far-away things look smooth. Like hills from the train window, all soft and green. Up close there are rocks."
"Mrs Rao let me feed the class fish today."
"See? A rock and a fish."

qa.q: What did Mrs Rao let Pankaj do today?
qa.a: Mrs Rao let Pankaj feed the class fish.

qa.q: Why does Pankaj remember only good things about the old school?
qa.a: Pankaj feels homesick for the old school, so bad days like standing outside or not getting passes have faded, and the old place feels nicer than it was.

qa.q: Which part of Uma's reply helped, and why?
qa.a: Uma said missing it was allowed before mentioning the rocks, so Pankaj didn't feel scolded and could admit the new school has good moments too.

qa.q: If you were Uma, what would you hope Pankaj notices next week?
qa.a: More good moments at the new school, like the fish, instead of only comparing it with a smoothed-out memory. 🙂

grounding: A child who changed schools praises the old teacher and team, while an older cousin gently recalls the quarrels and slights now forgotten.

passage: When we moved to Pune, I told everyone my old class in Bhopal was the best class in the whole world. Nobody fought. Everybody shared tiffin. The teacher smiled all day. Then Gautam, my old bench partner, did a video call. I said, "I miss our class so much." He said, "Me too. Remember when you and Rohit didn't talk for a whole month? And you cried because someone spilled ink on your chart?" I stopped. I had forgotten all of that. It was like the fights had fallen out of my head. My new class is a bit noisy. Maybe my old one was too. I'm Jaya, and I still miss it, but maybe not every part.

qa.q: Who did Jaya not talk to for a whole month in the old class?
qa.a: Rohit.

qa.q: Why did Jaya stop when Gautam mentioned the fights?
qa.a: Jaya was surprised, because those quarrels had slipped out of memory and the old class had felt perfect.

qa.q: What could Jaya try now that the old class doesn't look quite so perfect?
qa.a: Jaya could give the noisy new class a fair chance, since the old one had its hard days too.

qa.q: What might Gautam feel when Jaya says the old class was perfect?
qa.a: Gautam misses Jaya too, but remembers the real class with its fights and tears, so he gently brings back the rough parts.

grounding: A child who moved schools remembers the old class as perfect until a friend reminds them of the quarrels.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 3C, Wednesday. Farhan joined us from a school in Lucknow three weeks ago. He is polite and bright, but most days he tells the class that in his old school "nobody ever fought," "the teacher gave stars every day," and "everyone was my best friend." Today, when two boys argued over a football, he said loudly, "This never happened in my old school." Some children felt hurt. At pickup I spoke with his mother. She smiled and said he used to come home upset about a boy who took his tiffin, and once begged not to go back. I think he misses it so much that the hard days have faded. Tomorrow I'll pair him with Kabeer for class jobs and ask him to draw his old school and his new one side by side. — Mr Naveen

qa.q: Which city did Farhan's old school sit in?
qa.a: Lucknow.

qa.q: Why might Farhan believe nobody ever fought in his old school?
qa.a: He misses it a lot, so the good parts feel bright while the hard days, like the tiffin trouble, have quietly faded from his mind.

qa.q: What next step did Mr Naveen choose, and how might it help Farhan settle?
qa.a: Pairing him with Kabeer for class jobs and drawing both schools side by side, so he builds new friendships and sees both places more fairly.

qa.q: How might the other children in 3C feel when Farhan praises his old school?
qa.a: Some feel hurt or compared unfairly, as if their class isn't good enough, which could make it harder for them to welcome him.

grounding: A teacher notices a child who moved schools praising his old class as perfect while forgetting the quarrels he once had there.
